title: Tectonic Plates
keyIdea: Earth's rocky outer shell, the crust together with the top of the mantle, is broken into huge pieces called tectonic plates. They rest on hot mantle rock that is solid but flows very slowly, and they move a few centimetres a year, about as fast as fingernails grow. Where plates pull apart, rising hot rock makes new crust. Where they push together, an ocean plate sinks under another plate or two continents crumple into mountains. Where they slide past each other, they stick and then jolt, causing earthquakes. Most earthquakes and volcanoes happen along plate boundaries.
familyTip: Trace the coasts of South America and Africa from an atlas or a printed map, cut them out and slide them together across the Atlantic. Then look up a map of recent earthquakes together: see how the dots line up in bands, like the Ring of Fire round the Pacific, and find which plate your home sits on.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: tap Earth's layers, pull and push plates, strain a fault until it jolts, fit South America to Africa, sort real places.

kid: Earth is made of layers, like a peach. The outside layer is the crust. It is thin and made of hard rock. The crust is cracked into giant pieces called tectonic plates. Some plates carry land and some carry ocean floor.

Under the plates is the mantle. It is very hot, but it is not runny lava. It is solid rock that can flow very, very slowly, like stiff putty. The plates rest on it and move. They creep about as fast as your fingernails grow, just a few centimetres a year.

Plates meet in three ways. Where they pull apart, hot rock rises up into the crack and cools to make new rock. Where they push together, one plate can sink under the other, or the land crumples up into mountains. Where they slide past each other, they get stuck, then slip with a jolt. That jolt is an earthquake.
South America and Africa fit together like jigsaw pieces. The same fossils are found on both. They were once joined, long ago, and the plates carried them apart.
adult: Ages 9 to 11. This supports NGSS 4-ESS2-2 (patterns in Earth's features: mountains, volcanoes and earthquakes along plate edges) and leads to MS-ESS2-3 (fossils, rocks and continent shapes as evidence of past plate motion). In England it links Key Stage 2 geography on volcanoes and earthquakes with Key Stage 3 science on the structure of the Earth. Facts were checked against the USGS book This Dynamic Earth and the British Geological Survey's plate tectonics pages. Key words: crust, mantle, core, tectonic plate, plate boundary, divergent, convergent, transform, subduction, trench, fault, continental drift, Pangaea.

The lab has seven steps. Children tap the crust and the mantle on a cut-away Earth and turn a years dial: at 2.5 cm a year a gap grows to 25 km in a million years. They pull two plates apart and watch rising rock make new sea floor. They push an ocean plate under a continent, forming a trench and a volcano, then push India into Asia to raise the Himalayas. They strain a fault until it jolts twice, fit South America back against Africa so the Mesosaurus fossils line up, and sort Iceland, the Himalayas, the San Andreas Fault, Japan and the Mid-Atlantic Ridge.

Common mistakes. The biggest is that plates float on a sea of liquid magma. The mantle is solid rock that flows very slowly, and magma forms only in small pockets where rock partly melts. Other slips: plates move quickly or not at all, a gap opens like a hole when plates pull apart, the continent plate sinks under the ocean plate, the Himalayas are volcanoes, and sliding plates move smoothly. Be careful with the word float: it is fine as a picture, but the plates are not on water.

practice.prompt: What is right under the tectonic plates?
choices: Hot solid rock that flows very slowly
practice.hint: In the lab, what did the mantle label say about the layer under the crust?
practice.explain: The plates rest on the mantle. It is hot, but it is solid rock that flows very slowly, not a sea of lava.

practice.prompt: A plate moves {r} cm each year. How many centimetres does it move in {n} years?
practice.hint: Each year adds {r} cm, so multiply {r} by the number of years, {n}.
practice.explain: {r} × {n} = {=r*n} cm. That is slow: over a whole human life a plate moves only a few metres.

practice.prompt: An ocean plate pushes into a continent plate. What happens?
choices: The ocean plate sinks under the continent
The continent sinks under the ocean plate
practice.hint: Which plate was thin and heavy for its size in the lab?
practice.explain: Ocean plates are denser, so the ocean plate sinks under the continent. A deep trench forms and melting rock feeds volcanoes.

practice.prompt: A plate moves 5 cm a year. There are 100 000 cm in 1 km. How many years does it take to move {k} km?
practice.hint: Find the years for 1 km first: 100 000 ÷ 5. Then multiply by {k}.
practice.explain: 1 km takes 100 000 ÷ 5 = 20 000 years, so {k} km takes 20 000 × {k} = {=k*20000} years.

practice.prompt: Plates slide past each other at the San Andreas Fault. How do they move?
choices: They pull apart and make new rock
practice.hint: What happened to the strain bar in the lab before each jolt?
practice.explain: The rough edges stick while strain builds up. When it is too much, the plates slip at once, and the ground shakes in an earthquake.

choices: Huge pieces of Earth's rocky outer shell
Floating islands on a sea of lava
pool.hint: Think of the cracks drawn in the outer layer of the cut-away Earth.
pool.explain: Tectonic plates are giant pieces of the crust and the top of the mantle. They fit together over the whole Earth.

pool.prompt: How fast do tectonic plates move?
pool.hint: Remember the years dial: how wide was the gap after one year?
pool.explain: Plates move a few centimetres a year, about as fast as fingernails grow. Over millions of years that adds up to oceans.

pool.prompt: What forms where two ocean plates pull apart?
pool.hint: What filled the crack when you dragged the plates apart?
pool.explain: Hot rock rises into the crack, cools and makes new sea floor, as at the Mid-Atlantic Ridge.

pool.hint: Neither continent sank. What did the land do instead?
pool.explain: When two continents push together, neither sinks, so the land crumples upward. The Himalayas are still rising.

pool.prompt: Why are the same Mesosaurus fossils found in Brazil and southern Africa?
choices: The two continents were once joined
The animals swam across the ocean
pool.hint: What happened to the fossils when the jigsaw pieces fitted?
pool.explain: Mesosaurus lived in lakes and could not cross an ocean. Its fossils match because the land was joined in Pangaea, then split.

pool.prompt: Where do most earthquakes and volcanoes happen?
pool.hint: Where were all five places in the boundary detective step?
pool.explain: They cluster along plate edges, such as the Ring of Fire round the Pacific. The middle of a plate is much quieter.

pool.prompt: Which place is on a boundary where plates pull apart?
pool.hint: Which clue said the island slowly gets wider?
pool.explain: Iceland sits on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, where the plates pull apart. The Himalayas and Japan are where plates push together.

pool.prompt: Which word names the layer the plates rest on?
pool.hint: It was the orange layer you tapped second.
pool.explain: The mantle is the thick layer of hot rock under the crust. The core is far deeper, and the atmosphere is the air above.

pool.prompt: The Atlantic widens about 2.5 cm a year. How many centimetres wider is it after {n} years?
pool.hint: Each year adds 2.5 cm. Multiply 2.5 by {n}: double {n}, then add half of {n}.
pool.explain: 2.5 × {n} = {=2.5*n} cm. In a million years the same speed adds up to 25 km.

pool.prompt: India's plate moves north about {r} cm a year. How many metres does it move in 1000 years? (100 cm = 1 m)
pool.hint: Find the centimetres first: {r} × 1000. Then divide by 100 to get metres.
